name: Songsterr
tagline: Interactive guitar, bass and drum tabs that play back in sync with a scrolling cursor, with speed control and looping.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The player is not the product. alphaTab is open source and will render and play a Guitar Pro file in your browser with a synced cursor, tempo slider and loop markers in an afternoon, so the software half of Songsterr is genuinely a one-shot build. What you cannot generate is half a million human transcriptions of real songs, each one tracked, timed, fingered and corrected by people who listened to the record. That corpus is both labor and a licensing position, and it is the entire reason anyone opens the site. Build the player, then notice you have nothing to put in it.
coreLoopDIY: Loads Guitar Pro files you already own, renders them as tab, and plays them back with a scrolling cursor, tempo control, A/B loop and per-track mute.
requirements: Guitar Pro files (.gp, .gp5, .gpx) you already own or transcribed yourself
A SoundFont file for playback (alphaTab ships a default)
whatYouLose: The catalog: hundreds of thousands of songs you did not transcribe and will not transcribe
Transcription accuracy and the correction pipeline behind it, including multiple revisions per song
Search, so finding 'that riff' means already having the file
Native iOS and Android apps for practicing away from a laptop
Any licensing cover at all, which matters the moment you share your build
moatNotes: Tab sites live or die on their relationship with publishers and on a transcription backlog that took years of paid human ears.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the subscription buys a library, not a feature set. You want to learn a specific song tonight, you search it, and a correct, playable, multi-track transcription appears with a cursor that stays on the beat. A self-hosted player gives you that only for songs someone has already transcribed into a file you happen to possess, which is a much smaller universe than it sounds. The paid tier mostly removes friction around that search-to-practice loop, and friction removal on a large corpus is the only thing a solo build cannot fake.
notes: The player is a one-sitting build with alphaTab; the library is not. The moat is the transcription corpus and the publisher licensing that lets it exist.
prompt:
Build a local, offline tab player web app called "TabDesk". No accounts, no backend API, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Vite + TypeScript + vanilla DOM (no React)
- alphaTab (@coderline/alphatab) for parsing, rendering and audio playback
- Plain CSS, dark theme, no UI framework
- localStorage for persistence, nothing else

What it does:
1. A file drop zone plus a file picker that accepts .gp, .gp3, .gp4, .gp5, .gpx and .musicxml. Files are read client side as ArrayBuffer and handed to alphaTab. Nothing uploads anywhere.
2. Render the score as tablature with standard notation toggleable. Use alphaTab's horizontal and page layout modes, switchable from a toolbar button.
3. Playback with the alphaTab synth: play, pause, stop, and a cursor that follows the active beat. Auto-scroll the viewport to keep the cursor visible.
4. Tempo slider from 25% to 150% of the original tempo, showing both the percentage and the resulting BPM.
5. A/B loop: click a bar to set loop start, shift-click to set loop end, then a Loop toggle that restricts playback to that range. Show the selected range highlighted.
6. Track list sidebar generated from the score: per-track mute, solo and volume. Include a metronome toggle and a count-in toggle.
7. A "Library" panel that remembers opened files using IndexedDB (store the raw bytes plus title and artist from the file metadata) so reopening the app does not require re-dropping files. Include a delete button per entry.
8. Per-file practice state in localStorage: last tempo, last loop range, last selected track, and a free-text notes box.
9. Keyboard shortcuts: space play/pause, [ and ] nudge tempo, L toggle loop, M metronome.

Explicitly out of scope: any song catalog, any search of remote sources, any scraping of tab sites, user accounts, sync, mobile native apps, audio-to-tab transcription.

No secrets are needed, but still create a .env.example and read nothing from it beyond an optional ALPHATAB_SOUNDFONT_URL path.

Ship a README that states plainly: this plays Guitar Pro files you already have, it does not find them for you.
